citation.author: Aroles, Jeremy and Küpers, Wendelin
citation.title: Towards an integral pedagogy in the age of 'digital Gestell': Moving between embodied co-presence and telepresence in learning and teaching practices

discipline: organization/management-education studies -- Heideggerian philosophy of technology (Gestell/Gelassenheit) applied to pedagogy; not phenomenology-of-mood or psychology of boredom
thesis: Digitalisation confronts universities and business schools with three interconnected challenges -- the shift from embodied co-presence to telepresence, the need to re-embody digital teaching and learning, and the need to re-purpose the aims of business-school education -- all of which the authors read through Heidegger's concepts of enframing (Gestell) and releasement (Gelassenheit); the prescriptive upshot is an 'integral pedagogy' cultivated through an ethos of 'engaged releasement' that lets teachers and learners move reflectively between embodied and digital(ised) forms.
sections: 1 Introduction (pp.757-759) -- COVID-19 context, phenomenological framing, three-challenge preview, article roadmap

2 Technologies, embodiment and learning: 'Digital Gestell' (pp.759-761) -- 2.1 the Heideggerian concept of enframing (definition, danger, critique via Verbeek 2005 and Ruin 2010); 2.2 embodiment and the multifaceted nature of technologies (Heidegger's neglect of the body; case for retaining Gestell)

3 Online teaching, learning and pedagogy (pp.761-762) -- 3.1 contextualising online learning; 3.2 embodiment and learning: a phenomenological perspective (dataism, datafication, learnification, machine behaviourism)

4 Challenge 1 -- Shifting from co-presence to telepresence (pp.762-764) -- Other and othering (peer-learning loss); Feeling, sensing and experiencing (lecture-as-theatre, non-verbal cues); Here and there (bi-localized simultaneity, far-but-close paradox)

5 Challenge 2 -- Re-embodying teaching and learning activities (pp.764-766) -- re-embodiment via post-phenomenology (Ihde, Verbeek) and homo faber; re-embodying online education via affect-shaping materials (Ward 2018)

6 Challenge 3 -- Re-purposing teaching in business schools (pp.766-768) -- Beyond reductionism (apparatus critique via Agamben 2009); Digitality and repurposing (integral pluralism, Wals's emancipatory pedagogy, Biesta's qualification/subjectification/socialisation)

7 Discussion (pp.768-770) -- moving between co- and telepresence (Han's homo digitalis); political implications of enframing/mediation (Beverungen et al. 2019); an ethos of releasement for the age of digital Gestell (Ingold's education of attention, Verbeek's politicized post-phenomenology)
8 Conclusion (pp.770-771) -- recap of the three challenges; releasement as ethical-political practice; closing call for integral pedagogical practices in the spirit of engaged releasement

constructs.label: monotony / meaninglessness
constructs.treatment: functional analogy only -- Gestell's homogenizing/regimenting effect on teaching ('increasingly regimented and homogeneous'); reductionist 'silo type' curricula reproducing 'more of the same' via prefabricated templates -- never named 'monotony' or linked to boredom research

constructs.label: flow / engagement (contrast pole)
constructs.treatment: closest direct treatment -- peer-learning/engagement diminished under telepresence; re-embodied online materials designed to make 'engagement and commitment to the learning process' possible again (Ward 2018); 'engaged releasement' proposed as the recovering ethos

constructs.label: attentional disengagement / meta-awareness
constructs.treatment: light, analogical only -- loss of eye-contact/non-verbal cues, susceptibility to 'external interruptions and distractions' in telepresence; not attention research

constructs.label: temporality of boredom (time-drag)
constructs.treatment: construct-adjacent but a DIFFERENT sense -- bi-localized simultaneity, 'community of time without... community of physical space,' the 'far-but-close' paradox; a temporality of dislocation/simultaneity, not boredom's stretched, dragging Zeitvertreib

constructs.label: profound/deep boredom (FCM 3rd form)
constructs.treatment: absent throughout -- not discussed, named, or cited

readings.summary: This source does not engage FCM's boredom analysis at all. Its Heideggerian apparatus is drawn from two later, different texts -- 'The Question Concerning Technology' (1977, source of Gestell) and 'Discourse on Thinking' (1966, source of Gelassenheit) -- neither of which the authors relate to mood, Befindlichkeit, Stimmung, or boredom. Direct search of the full extraction confirms the words 'boredom,' 'mood,' and 'attunement' do not appear anywhere in the article. No bridges-to-fcm edge is warranted; forcing one would misrepresent the source.

concepts: far-but-close paradox of perceived proximity (Wilson et al. 2008)
learnification / datafication / dataism (Biesta; Williamson et al.; Beer)
interlocutors: Martin Heidegger (1977 The Question Concerning Technology; 1966 Discourse on Thinking) -- primary conceptual source (Gestell, Gelassenheit), NOT the Being and Time / FCM mood-analysis
Don Ihde (1990, 2009, 2012; with Malafouris 2019) -- postphenomenology, technological embodiment, homo faber
Peter-Paul Verbeek (2005, 2020; with Rosenberger 2015) -- postphenomenology; critiques Gestell as abstract/nostalgic; politicized postphenomenology
Giorgio Agamben (2009) -- apparatus concept applied to business-school curricula
Arjen Wals (2020) -- emancipatory, relational sustainability pedagogy
Hartmut Rosa (2013) -- social acceleration, collapsing spatio-temporal frames
Byung-Chul Han (2017) -- homo digitalis, In the Swarm
Dan Ward (2018) -- Dreyfus/Merleau-Ponty-inflected bodily affective understanding in online learning
Kevin Aho (2005, 2010) -- cited on Heidegger's neglect of the body ONLY, not on melancholia/boredom; same author as Strand-A bor-sec-01
Fred Schalow (2006) -- Heidegger and the body
Andreas Beverungen, Timon Beyes, Lisa Conrad (2019) -- organizational powers of digital media
tensions: Gestell retained despite conceded critique: Verbeek (2005) calls the concept 'too abstract and/or too nostalgic' and Ruin (2010) charges it with monolithic characterisations of technology; A&K concede this (p.760) but retain Gestell anyway, reframing the task as what Heideggerian thinking offers the 21st century (Georgakis and Ennis 2014) rather than defending empirical fidelity.

Epochal/totalizing Gestell vs. pluralistic post-phenomenology: the article yokes Heidegger's monolithic, epoch-defining enframing to Ihde/Verbeek's anti-essentialist, technology-specific post-phenomenology (human-prostheses inter-relations, p.765) without fully reconciling the difference in analytical grain between the two frameworks.

Telepresence as loss vs. telepresence as a different (not lesser) embodiment: Challenge 1 stresses what 'gets lost' in disembodied telepresence (pp.761-764), while Challenge 2 insists 'cyberspace is not a disembodied reality' (p.765) and reframes the same phenomenon as a different kind of embodiment -- the article holds both framings without settling which is primary.
Reductionist, apparatus-governed business-school pedagogy vs. proposed relational/emancipatory integral pedagogy (Wals 2020; Biesta) -- the central opposition structuring Challenge 3 (pp.766-768).

Cross-cluster note for later Strand-B linking: none of Feldges, Mertel, Standish, or Thomson (bor-sec-16 through bor-sec-19) appear in this source's ~90-item reference list; any future cross-linking would have to run through shared secondary literature (Ihde, Verbeek, Biesta, Heidegger's technology essays) rather than direct citation. Kevin Aho (Strand-A bor-sec-01 author) IS cited here, but only on embodiment, not on melancholia/boredom.
